title: Lab: Algorithms
contentHTML:
Theory of Computation:

Models of computation in CS primarily rest upon the ideas of Turing Machines and Lambda Calculus. Imperative programming paradigms like Procedural and Object-Oriented programming largely trace their lineage to the Turing Machine. The Turing Machine model of computation consists of a global state that is modified by the flow of execution through a sequence of commands (e.g. like following a recipe or driving directions)

Declarative programming paradigms like Functional and Logic programming languages naturally arose out of Lambda Calculus. The Lambda Calculus model of computation is ideally stateless wherein data flows through a sequence of formulas/rules to produce a return value (e.g. like a spreadsheet or SQL). A passing familiarity with these two intellectual traditions helps to understand the fundamental thought patterns embedded in computational thinking and the various problem spaces wherein each would be most appropriate.

We also explore other models for representing computational thought independent from the flows of execution through commands (Imperative) or data through rules (Declarative). Finite State Machines are a state-based style of computation often used to design simple but reliable hardware devices (e.g. vending machines). Some believe that Cellular Automata is the best model for modeling the computation inherent in all matter and physical systems from geological processes to biological cells. From the ancient Greek celestial gear mechanisms to the millions of lines of code in modern cars we see the computational algorithms date back thousands of years and are rapidly proliferating throughout the world today.

  • Lambda Calculus (Stanford and Eval as Trees)
  • Turning Machine (BrainF and BrainF Interpreter)
  • RegEx FSM Simulator
  • Cellular Automata

Algorithms and Design Patterns:

These exercises are to expose you to general algorithmic thinking for particular tasks like searching and sorting. If time permits, we'll also expand on the concept of patterns in software with idioms as well as larger canonical software design patterns accepted as best practices for common software tasks under various paradigms.

  • Visualgo.net: TSP and Bubble Sort
  • Algorithm-Visualizer.org (Visualization + Code)
  • Algomation.com (Visualization + Code)
  • Problem-Solving with Algorithms and Data Structures (Ch.2 Analysis)
  • Design Patterns on PythonAnywhere.com

Programming Paradigms:

As we'll see, typical computational thought decomposes thinking into unnaturally small discrete steps that do not map seamlessly onto human thinking. Most humans tend to organically think and speak in inexact terms at generally higher levels of abstraction typical of Natural Languages. In contrast, programming languages are Artificial Languages designed to reduce communication to a narrow, unambiguous and efficient mode of expression more akin to mathematics than English.

We demonstrate several programming languages at different levels of abstraction from theoretical Turing Machines to Machine/Assembly to several high-level languages. This is designed to help students more naturally think at multiple levels of abstraction to better bridge the gulf between Natural Languages and Programming Languages that can make programming so difficult at first.

Finally, we introduce and demonstrate several algorithms across very different programming paradigms. This serves several purposes: (a) illustrate the intellectual history and interdependence of artificial intelligence across multiple fields in the Humanities, (b) introduce students to multiple cognitive paradigms to expand their intellectual toolset and outlook, and (c) concretely demonstrating the 'No Free Lunch' Theory by showing how problems impractical under one paradigm can be trivial under another (and visa-versa).

Object-Oriented Programming (@10:24): (Ruby Quickstart)

class CashRegister
attr_reader :drawer

def initialize
@drawer = [2000, 1000,
500, 100,
25, 10,
5, 1]
end

def make_change owed, tendered
difference = tendered - owed

change = []
i = 0
denomination = @drawer[i]

while difference > 0 do
if difference < denomination
i += 1
denomination = @drawer[i]
next
end

change << denomination
difference -= denomination
end

change
end
end

title: Topic: Algorithms (Fall 2020)
contentHTML:
This week we learn about the origins of computer science dating back to Aristotle and influenced by the fields of both logic and linguistics. We'll also explore the connections that are being made between human cognition and and computers. Is human cognitive processing algorithmic?

In terms of code, we'll learn how Computer Science represents and implements one familiar aspect of cognition: algorithmic thinking. We'll study this with examples of specific algorithms (e.g. search) and a general pattern of computation (e.g. recursion).  We'll also explore measures of algorithmic space-time complexity through BigO notation.

We close the week by focusing on the one aspect of human cognition that is still a mystery: consciousness. Can consciousness be explained mathematically, materially, or spiritually? Will science ever be able to explain consciousness, or is the qualitative nature of experience unquantifiable?

﻿

title: Topic: Artificial Intelligence (2021)
contentHTML:
Week Fourteen: Artificial Intelligence

Before our final project, we'll look at what some speculate may be humankind's 'last great invention': Artificial Intelligence (AI). Neuroscience provides the only model of advanced intelligence in our universe, and recent advances in AI have developed neural nets modeled on the neural pathways of the brain. We'll explore original Artificial Neuron (AN) inspirations from neuroscience as well as the growing cross-pollination between AI and Neuroscience. Then we'll discuss what it means as our computers increasingly become 'smarter' than us by more metrics in a growing number of diverse fields (including playing Go, protein folding, poker, language translation, programming, medical diagnosis, writing, and art).

Next we'll reflect again on the nature of intelligence and consciousness. Can machines "think" and will we be able to model human consciousness in silica? Finally, we'll conclude with the international AI arms race, as well as a discussion of a possible existential threat. What solutions can we offer from the perspective of the liberal arts and our humanistic tradition? Should we have a greater say, earlier, in the development and implementation of AI?

title: Topic: Artificial Intelligence 2025
contentHTML:
In this, our final week, we look at what some speculate may be humanity's last great invention: Artificial Intelligence (AI). We'll see how AI has rapidly grown to be a central focus in academia, industry and even politics. 

We'll take a brief look at the history of AI, measure the accelerating pace of innovation, and return to questions we raised in the first weeks of class. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are introduced, with parallels drawn between both simple and complex models of human neurophysiology. After 60 years of divergence, we're now seeing a synthesis of approaches and discoveries between AI and neuroscience of the human brain (the most sophisticated model of intelligence in our known universe).

We'll ask some of the questions with which we began this course in September: What is intelligence? And what is consciousness? Then we'll consider whether a machine can be either intelligent or conscious. Finally, we'll consider two very different positions on the rise of AI: the fear of extreme existential risk, as well as the promise of a better, more intelligently-organized world.

title: Topic: Bioinformatics
contentHTML:
Bioinformatics - Hacking Human Biology with Big Data and Computational Models

In our penultimate week we explore a computational interpretation of biology as an information processing system. We'll understand why a computational model of cellular life is, in terms of data, orders of magnitude more complex than any computational or mathematical model we've seen so far. 

We'll also see how the unique challenges of bioinformatics require high-performance computational and large-scale statistical methods to study genomics--one of the original big data applications. Bioinformatics and computational biology have revolutionized our understanding of genetics, medicine and life thanks in large part to rapid advances in computer science: big data, computational power and improved algorithms. 

As in other weeks, we see how rapid progress in technology is poised to challenge the very nature of humanity.  Forty years ago test tube baby technologies like IVF were new, controversial and pushing the limits of medical ethics at the time. Despite initial attempts to limit access to the procedure, today approximately 10% of all births in Denmark are born with assisted reproductive technology like IVF.

The fictional world depicted in the 1997 film Gattaca is fast becoming a reality.  For the cost of a few thousand dollars, parents could practice statistical 'soft' eugenics by fertilizing multiple eggs, testing each for desirable traits across a million SNPs, and selecting only the 'best' one for implantation. How can society prevent the resulting massive, permanent, and accelerating biological inequality irreversibly separating the 'haves' from the 'have-nots'? Other technologies also stand poised to change what it means to be human forever, most notably attempts to "cure" aging. Finally, biotechnology has the potential to bring much good, but it also has the potential to sow much harm through the creation of new and previously unimaginably lethal bioweapons.

title: Topic: Bioinformatics (2019)
contentHTML:
Bioinformatics - Genetics and Molecular Biology
M Class:            Computational Biology, Molecular Biology and Genetics
W Lab:                Drug Discovery and Designer Proteins
F Discussion:    Eugenics, Transhumanism and Immortality

In our second week on Algorithms we noted the computational perspective of living cells as information processing systems. In essence, we are physical computational systems based upon carbon and chemistry rather than silicon and electromagnetism. 

In our penultimate week we more directly explore this computational interpretation of cellular life as information processing systems via the forms, functions and interactions of DNA, mRNA and proteins.  We'll understand why a computational model of cellular life is orders of magnitude more complex than any computational or mathematical models we've seen so far. The information, behaviors and feedbacks between just these three elements alone account for practically uncountable levels of constantly shifting, overlapping, interacting and dynamically self-modifying networks.

We also see how the unique challenges of bioinformatics require high-performance computational and large-scale statistical methods to study various -omics - perhaps the original big data application along with high-energy particle physics (c.f. LHC).  In particular, we'll study the inherently high-dimensional problem of protein folding and learn approaches to this seemingly intractable problem. Progress in this area holds immense potential in drug discovery, gene therapy and personalized medicine as well as in growing crop yields, securing clean water and fighting climate change.

Along with AI and Neuroscience, Genomics is one of the rapidly evolving fields today and all three overlap with the core content of our course. All these fields have been revolutionized by rapid advances in big data, computational power and improved algorithms. In this class we explore how Neuroscience and AI both illuminate key aspects of humanity related to perception, language, intelligence, identity, sociability, economics, bias, ethics, consciousness, etc. This week we'll see how Genomics explains the scaffolding that underlies all these higher order levels of humanity as well as the very foundations of our physical existence.

As in other weeks, we see how rapid progress in technology is poised to challenge the very nature of humanity.  Forty years ago test tube babies technologies like IVF were new and controversial. Despite previous attempts to limit access to the procedure, today approximately 10% of all births in Denmark are born with assisted reproductive technology like IVF.

Today, for the cost of a few thousand dollars, mothers can practice statistical eugenics by fertilizing multiple eggs, testing each for desirable traits, and only implanting the 'best' one.  Last year Chinese researcher He Jiankui applied established CRISPR procedures to edit the genes of twin baby girls making them and their descendants resistant to HIV. This was not a technical breakthrough but rather a crossing of the ethical rubicon in performing these precision genetic edits on heritable human germline cells. How can humanity deal with what seems the inevitable opening of this potential Pandora's Box of eugenics and the consequences that could arise from it like massive, permanent and accelerating inequality?

In addition to genetic engineering, we'll also touch upon areas of drug discovery, systems biology, anti-aging and the Transhumanism / Singularity movement. Given the potential diversity of backgrounds and topics this week we'll again rely upon a variety of shorter videos to capture the broad gestalt of specific topics as well as demonstrate the important connections between them.

Videos and animations are perhaps the ideal format to quickly intuit many of the complicated and interrelated concepts and processes we explore this week. Despite my best screening, inevitably there will be some specialized terminology/concepts in parts of these videos, so focus on capturing the overall concepts and interrelationships rather than details. Practice the valuable skill of reading just beyond the edge of you comprehension/comfort level and eliding over details to grasp the bigger picture of these videos (intellectual grit).

NOTE: We'll cover the essentials of cellular biology, genetics and proteonomics that you need to know in class Monday.  Unfortunately, ours is such an unusual course that I could not find a concise summary of these three topics within a single, well-explained and tractable video of reasonable length speaking at a level of abstraction appropriate for our class.

You are not expected to memorize nor master the many detailed bio concepts. Friday's Quiz will focus on a balance between the general big ideas of selected readings (e.g. the Central Dogma of Molecular Biology representing information flow) yet specific enough that they cannot be guessed without doing the reading. Do not stress over the details and feel free to put a 'black box' around the points in the readings that go too far into the weeds

title: Topic: Data (2021)
contentHTML:
Data, especially Big Data, has been called the "new oil." This is why data, along with an intimate understanding of its forms, is the introduction to our course.

We begin by exploring how humans and computers encode data differently. Philosophers have long debated whether there is a reality beyond sensory data. How do we know what we know, and do we need data, whether sensory or numeric, for knowledge?

Next we compare how humans encode data--using perception and memory--to how computers encode data. In both cases there is "loss," but the reasons are different. With computers, we can understand how information is stored--using compression--by recourse to information theory and entropy (watch out! Information entropy is subtlety different from the entropy you may already be familiar with from physics).

There is another key idea this week--the possibility that information, rather than matter, may form the basis of all reality. While we tend to think of "data" as inert, however, information is not. We'll see how the internal structure of data can produce misleading statistical measurements with Anscombe's Quartet. The Monty Hall problem will illustrate how our fundamentally flawed our intuitions on probability can be using computer simulation.

Finally, we explore the larger picture. We can often be identified by just a few pieces of information, and some suggest that with 300 likes an algorithm can know you better than yourself. Are we data? What elements of being "you" are unquantifiable? We also consider Dataism, and whether, as Harari suggests, it's our new god. Does Dataism solve the limitations of more traditional methods of knowing? Harari makes a particularly provocative claim about fighting an "old war." What's the story he tells? Do you think he's right?

DataCamp exercises offer a more traditional way of understanding Data Science, and these courses provide foundational concepts and skills that will be re-contextualized in our Data Humanities class. This week's Data Science for Everyone introduces many terms that we'll return to in future weeks--the Internet of Things, Databases, Data Visualization, Descriptive Statistics, Modeling and Forecasting, and A/B Testing are just a few. We have a whole course devoted to Machine Learning and Deep Learning--here you'll get just a brief overview.

title: Topic: Data Science
contentHTML:
Data Science - Bias and Fairness
M Class:            Clustering Algorithms and scikit-learn Pipeline
W Lab:              Linear Regression, Decision Trees and Confusion Matrix
F Discussion:    Bias and Fairness in Data and Models

This week we'll explore the science of constructing statistical models that use data to capture, explain, predict and potentially change outcomes in the world around us. Unlike last week's focus on NLP using unstructured textual data, this week we study Data Science which builds computational models based upon structured numeric data. The practice of Data Science is becoming ubiquitous and the Python library scikit-learn is arguably the most popular library for DS.

The social question this week relates to the growing power, use and accuracy of data over humans. With ever more powerful hardware, efficient algorithms and massive datasets, our models demonstratively outperform humans in a growing range of fields with broad and/or deep impact.  These data models are increasingly deployed to make or assist decision making for medical diagnosis, loans, college admissions, hiring, criminal sentencing, predictive policing, and identifying and or killing combatants in war. 

What are the limits of this shifting border between human responsibility and machines capability as our moral and legal subrogates? As accuracy generally correlates to complexity, how can fairness, accuracy and transparency (FAT) be built into our models in the face of powerful economic incentives to automate costly, unreliable, inconsistent and sometimes malicious humans out of the decision-making process? How will the overall trend towards machine models and work automation affect economics, law and politics much less social structure and individual psychology. How to we shape those changes to the benefit of humanity instead of the benefit of fewer and fewer who are increasingly distanced from humanity in terms of wealth, education and socialization?

  • How do you feel about machine learning increasingly making for you and for society at large (e.g. predictive policing and AI-assisted judicial sentencing guidelines).
  • We read a number of articles that raise concerns about bias embedded in the data and algorithms behind machine learning.  What about the bias, irrationality and inconsistency inherent in human judgement? Is it possible that machines are still less bias than humans?
  • If studies show that one could develop a machine learning system less biased than human judgement, should society hand over all such decisions to machine learning systems?
  • Where machine learning systems make important decisions over humans, there is always a potential for bias and outright fraud to creep in by governments, hackers or private companies who own/control the data/algorithms/systems that run the machine learning systems.  How could society best ensure that such systems are not corrupted, either intentionally or unintentionally?
  • As the technology of such machine learning systems becomes increasingly complex, these systems hold the promise of ever improving performance and fairness.  At the same time, the number of people who could accurately inspect and judge the fairness of such systems would shrink.  At what point, if any, should society limit the sophistication and benefits of such machine learning systems to ensure there are a minimal number of people who can judge the fairness and accuracy of such systems?
  • Currently the vast majority of data, algorithms and systems that implement machine learning are held as private property by large corporations and protected as proprietary trade secrets and intellectual property.  In the cases where these machine learning systems are making wide-ranging life decisions over many individuals in society, should there be some transparency and/or government regulation?  Where should the line be drawn between private property rights over the machine learning systems and government regulation in the name of individual civil rights?

title: Topic: Evolving Life
contentHTML:
If we view humans from a computational perspective, we can see living cells as information processing systems that execute DNA code to create proteins using a complex biochemical operating system. We are built from a massively parallel computational system based on carbon and chemistry rather than silicon and electromagnetism.

This week, we explore biology as an information processing system. We'll understand why a computational model of cellular life is orders of magnitude more complex than any model we've seen so far. The information, behaviors, processing pathways and feedbacks in overlapping and interconnected systems create constantly shifting and dynamically self-modifying networks. These networks are embedded within each other, inter-operate alongside and between each other and run simultaneously with distinct signaling at different levels of resolution.

We also see how the unique challenges of bioinformatics require high-performance computational and large-scale statistical methods to study genomics--one of the original big data applications (which also includes astrophysics and experimental subatomic physics). Bioinformatics and computational biology have revolutionized our understanding of genetics, medicine and life thanks in large part to rapid advances in computer science: big data, computational power and improved algorithms. 

As in other weeks, we see how rapid progress in technology is poised to challenge the very nature of humanity.  Forty years ago, test tube baby technologies like IVF were new, controversial, and pushed the limits of medical ethics. Despite initial attempts to limit access to the procedure, today approximately 10% of all births in Denmark are born with assisted reproductive technology like IVF.

The fictional world depicted in the 1997 film Gattaca is fast becoming a reality.  For the cost of a few thousand dollars, parents can practice statistical 'soft' eugenics by fertilizing multiple eggs, testing each for desirable traits across a million SNPs, and selecting the 'best' one for implantation. How can society prevent a massive, permanent, and accelerating biological inequality from a man-made speciation event that could fundamentally separate the 'haves' from the 'have nots'?

This week also raises a number of questions about genetic engineering, precision medicine, creating deadly new bioagents (for academic, commercial and military ends), and the quest to "cure" aging. Once again, computation applied to a domain (that of life itself) results in possibilities that are both incredibly promising and terrifying.

Unfortunately, Datacamp does not offer concise exercises in bioinformatics, computational biology,  or genomics, and these approaches would also require a fair amount of domain knowledge. Instead, we'll continue our Datacamp exercises building a foundation in statistical thinking. We'll also begin some real-world applications of the methods you've learned, for example analyzing a TV dataset. (Note: there is an intro to datacamp projects you can scroll through if you're finding it difficult to figure out what to do)

title: Topic: Simulations
contentHTML:
Simulations

Over half a century of Moore's Law has enabled powerful new computational approaches. These can create and run simulations of complex models on massive datasets. Unlike models in introductory physics and engineering, models for many interesting phenomena (for example, predicting elections or modeling personality) cannot be reduced to analytical equations with tractable solutions. In such situations, computers allow us to surface key latent relationships that would otherwise be impossible to detect, quantify and model. Even for noisy data riddled with outliers, voids and shifting distributions in the statistical properties of big data (combined with various techniques like regularization and massive new modeling paradigms like deep neural networks) can clarify, extract and model key features, complex relationships and predict the evolution of systems over time.

This week we'll focus on a few important dynamic models that explicitly add the dimension of time to our models from last week: disease outbreaks, human behavior (the evolution of trust), women and promotion. We'll extend the REDCAPE multimodal way of thinking from last week to see how human behavior can be modeled, predicted and changed by technology. This helps lay the foundation for our upcoming week on social networks.

Tuesday starts with a slightly deeper dive into the theory and practice of statistics. We'll also begin our exploration of modeling humans and learn about network models and models of value and power. We'll discuss ways very slight differences in behaviors (i.e. the evaluation of female workers) can lead to very large discrepancies in outcomes. Thursday we'll simulate disease outbreaks. We'll use game theory simulations to witness how trust can slowly spread like a contagion despite clear incentives for short-term betrayals and other immediate self-optimization strategies. We'll also consider the ways Machine Learning might create new and better opportunities to address a problem with large organizations/governments. (Scroll to the bottom for instructions on mini-project #2).

Miniproject#2 One week from today (November 18th). Possible 3 day extension max. 

The goal of this project is a) to explore the complexity of fitting a model to your text, b) experiment with tuning via smoothing and window size and c) find a non-obvious story in the data. Please put graphs and interpretation with specific references to text/cruxes and peaks in a word doc and upload to Moodle.

Below are questions to answer:

1) Explore at least two DIFFERENT models  (note VADER and TEXTBLOB are often quite similar so don't compare unless they diverge significantly) and decide which of the two works best. Give an example of at least one peak or valley as evidence for this decision. You can look around the line numbers of differences in peaks and valleys to make a quick call (note earlier in the notebook each line of text is given a number--look there). 

2) Explore at least two smoothing algorithms (sma, exponential, savtisky-golay) and give an example of at least one peak or valley to justify why one is better than the other.

3) Explore at least two different hyperparameters  (i.e. default and a different option; rule of thumb: you will want to try smaller for a very large text, larger for a smaller text) for your smoothing method of choice. Again, give an example of why one seems to work better than another using evidence.

REMEMBER points near neutral may not be significant, and models may not do well with the beginning and end of the novel where there is less data to produce a strong signal).

NOTE: in an ideal world this process would be iterative, or you would actually try each model with each smoothing. HOWEVER, here we're just trying to get a sense of differences in models/smoothing algorithms/hyperparameters. 

4) Analyze at least 2 significant peaks and 2 valleys. REMEMBER that the capital letters signify the actual peak or valley, but you are averaging/smoothing the graph, so this is approximate rather than exact. Do the peaks and valleys comport with your predicted graph? Which cruxes did you not predict? What, if anything, does the model miss? 

5) What is the story in your model? What did you notice from the emotional arc that is non-obvious?  (In other words, although all models are wrong, what is useful here for understanding the way the text works?)

For examples of method and analysis feel free to consult Section 2 and Section 3 of The Shapes of Stories. I wrote the book in 2021 and it was published in 2022. Since then we have explored using LLMs and other smoothing methods (like savitsky-golay), which I would encourage you to try if you'd like to use sentiment analysis for a final project. We will have a library with the ability to use an LLM available for your final project if you'd like try to a state-of-the-art approach. I have been very impressed with some of them--they are tend to be more accurate, although even the simpler models often do quite well as long as your text is not overly complex, satirical, ironic, etc.

title: Topic: Social Networks 2025
contentHTML:
In earlier weeks, we set the groundwork for understanding network and graph theory, as well as rational actor and cooperative game theory. This week we integrate a number of previous concepts to consider the influence of social networks and the ways in which humans operate outside rational actor norms.

We start with a number of ideas that challenge assumptions underlying rational actor behavior: cognitive biases, the power of emotion, and biological aspects of behavior that call into question the very notion of free will itself. 

We'll then consider techniques to capture, model and exploit human emotions and social behavioral patterns using network theory and graph theory. We'll explore at a few examples of social network analysis in TV shows: The Song of Ice and Fire and Friends. In class, we'll do a bit of a deeper dive into exploring social media networks.

All of this background leads up to discussion: are we being hacked by our technology or can we program humanity into our tools? Tristan Harris made his name arguing for a more careful relationship to our tools lest they "hack" us. Yuval Harari also worries about our "hacked" humanity, most notably because the notions of "rational" humanity inherited from the Enlightenment underpin our political theory of democracy. Is this conception of what it means to be human out of date?

This week gives us the final set of tools you'll need to complete your final project. We will be introduced to NetworkX--focus on the concepts, as we will rely on Gemini to help us code your miniproject #3. Remember to have your screenplay or play ready for Tuesday.

As a reminder, here are your choices for a final project. Begin thinking about what you'd like to do, and please check digital kenyon iphs 200 for ideas.

  1. Finding a story in data (using Tableau or Python)
  2. Exploring a text (novels, scripts, social media, news, financial text, etc) using sentiment analysis (in special cases you can also try topic modeling, however you will need to learn the theory behind it)
  3. Social network analysis (again, you may need to spend more time reviewing the various ways to explore networks).
  4. Exploring the ethics of a current technology with detailed attention to the technology itself. NOTE: Earlier feedback on your sentiment analysis and Tableau projects is to guide you on your final projects. Earlier feedback should guide you as to ways you would need to improve were you to select that option for a final project and hope to receive an A.
